newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialist Jospin appeals to women voters.
newsitem.headline: French Socialist Jospin appeals to women voters.

text.p: French Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin reached out to female voters on Wednesday with a pledge to give important cabinet portfolios to women if the left won France's May 25-June 1 parliamentary election.
"If there is a government of change, then it will be a government in which women will have major posts," Jospin told a news conference.

However, he insisted that the women in his government not be referred to as "Jospinettes", saying he had been shocked by the media's use of the term "Juppettes" for the women in the cabinet of conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
"I would personally hope that this type of term would not be used again," he said.

The Socialists are fighting an uphill battle in the two-round election for the National Assembly, with final voter surveys showing the governing centre-right in the lead but the left within reach of an upset victory.
Opinion polls also showed the Socialists lagging behind the centre-right in the eyes of women voters.

The surveys have consistently found a so-called gender gap, with a significantly greater proportion of women than men favouring centre-right parties and a greater proportion of men than women favouring the Socialists.
In an effort to close the gap -- as well as to increase the clout of women in parliament -- both Socialists and Communists have introduced quotas of women candidates for the election.
About 30 percent of candidates in each party are women.

Jospin appeared at the party news conference surrounded by many of the Socialists' most high-profile women, including former cabinet ministers Elisabeth Guigou, Martine Aubry and Frederique Bredin and Strasbourg mayor Catherine Trautmann.
"Clearly, none of us likes this term (Jospinettes), even though we all love Lionel," Aubry told reporters.
Jospin said periods of Socialist rule had been kind to France's women while there had been setbacks for women during rightist governments.
Juppe came to office in May 1995 after the election of conservative President Jacques Chirac trumpeting a record 12 women in the cabinet, or 30 percent of his ministers.
But he sacked eight of them in a reshuffle later that year, cutting the percentage of women ministers to an unexceptional 13 percent.
